Alan Black who had come in as reserve to take the place of Barrie Sawyer, who was suffering from a bad cold, ran well to take us up to 2nd place, about 10 secs. ahead of Walton, but Portsmouth through Martin Hyman, opened up a big lead on this leg of 4½ miles.

This created a situation which in recent years has become a familiar pattern to Gerry North - chasing the agile form of Martin Hyman! The Portsmouth runner's lead was slowly whittled away but, for all his effort, Gerry could only peg back 18 seconds of the lost half minute.

Alan Black pulled back nineteen seconds across Gatwick Airport with a stylish performance which gained him the second fastest time of the day, and Gerry North set of on the long trek to Handcross to Handcross with Martin Hyman in sight.
Charlie Dabbs was first off into the second half of the race and although he was 8 seconds slower than Lonnen(Bristol) he was only 10secs away from Martin Hyman's stage record.

That hero of the Brighton Road, Charlie Walker, fought hard to hold his place on the next leg but Weatherill was 23 seconds faster on the day and Tony Fairclough took off (almost literally) on stage 9,thirteen seconds behind the imposing Martin Hyman.

We arrived in Mexico City on November 7th 1965 accompanied by Martin Hyman and John Cooke (Portsmouth), Dominic Keily (Derby) and Mike Turner (Liverpool) together with John Le Masurier, the team coach, and Doctors Pugh and Owen.

Score now 169 as against Portsmouth's 155, for whom Martin Hyman was moving through the field from 80th place at a great speed. Towards the end of the 2nd lap Gerry had moved up to 3rd with Thresher 17th, Geoff North 22nd, Fairclough 26th, Thorpe 39th and Dabbs 45th,totalling 152.
Martin Hyman was Portsmouth's sole representative in the '2' and he was beaten by A.Smith for the Bels., another of the Kerr-Reilly-Barrow clan from Victoria Pk. in Scotland.

With only 15 points separating the Portsmouth and Belgrave teams, the battle really hotted up on the second circuit but our rivals got the better of the exchanges - mainly due to that fine team runner, Martin Hyman.

Gerry's efforts however took their toll over this pleasant but undulating course, and approximately half a mile from home Martin Hyman who till then had been 'sitting in ' opened up a lead which Gerry was unable to close as they came back onto the track.
Gerry looked good, but one wondered whether someone had kidded him it was the 'three' - if they had, it was probably Martin Hyman, who was anchoring the field a full straight behind.

A regular pre-race routine gives a feeling of confidence and reduces the possibility of upsets resulting from unexpected changes in routine. Finally, I would like to thank Martin Hyman, Bruce Tulloh, Dr. Pugh and his research team for their interest and expert guidance.
